question: Directive (EU) 2024/12751 on the energy performance of buildings requires Member States to improve the energy class of the building stock and will ultimately prohibit the rental of the worst-performing properties.

In several Member States, including France, these rules are already resulting in huge numbers of properties being withdrawn from the rental market, as the owners cannot afford to pay for the renovations required. According to the French national monitoring centre for energy renovation2, 1.
6 million homes could become impossible to rent by 2028, compounding a housing crisis already marked by a 55 % hike in house prices and a 27 % increase in rents since 2010 (Eurostat, 2024)3. 1.

Has the Commission really assessed what impact the directive concerned is having on access to housing, particularly for young people, low-income families and the elderly, who were identified as the most vulnerable groups in the European Parliament’s report on housing affordability problems across socio-demographic groups4?

Does the Commission see a major contradiction with the European Green Deal here, in that Brussels, in pushing through its technocratic climate transition, is forcing the Member States to adopt uniform rules that have nothing to do with social and territorial reality?
Is it intending to introduce a flexibility clause to allow Member States to tailor these rules to suit their specific economic and social circumstances?

Directive (EU) 2024/1275 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 on the energy performance of buildings (recast). May 2023 report on poor energy performance in private rental buildings as at 1 January 2022, French national monitoring centre for energy renovation, Ministry of Ecological Transition and Territorial Cohesion: https://www.statistiques.developpement-durable.gouv.

fr/les-passoires-energetiques-du-parc-locatif-prive-au1er-janvier-2022-0 Eurostat (2024), House price index – quarterly data (prc_hpi_q) and housing cost overburden rate by region (ilc_lvho07). European Parliament, Housing affordability problems across socio-demographic groups, October 2025.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) The recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1 does not ban the renting of worst-performing buildings, nor does it impose obligations to renovate individual residential buildings. In line with the Better Regulation principles, the recast EPBD was preceded by an impact assessment.

This showed that the worst-performing residential buildings are often occupied by vulnerable households and that the proposed measures will help reduce their energy bills. Energy costs represent a major share of households’ overall living costs.

Renovating dwellings that are in poor condition, including those with poor energy performance, will improve access to decent, sustainable and affordable housing, particularly for low-income households, as highlighted in the European Affordable Housing Plan published by the Commission in December 20252.

Rather than imposing uniform rules, the recast EPBD gives Member States significant flexibility to address social and territorial specificities and challenges, including through tailored national measures and financial incentives.

Member States can also rely on EU funding instruments, such as the Recovery and Resilience Facility3, the Social Climate Fund4 and the Cohesion policy Funds5, to support building renovations. As announced in the Affordable Housing Plan, the Commission will put forward a housing simplification package to facilitate the supply of affordable and sustainable housing.
